turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning, Mrs Hale. I'll do your blood pressure before Dr Okonkwo comes in. That's 138 over 84, pulse 72.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): 138? Oh. Is that bad? I go all funny in these places, look, my hands are shaking.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): It's an ordinary clinic reading, love. My sister's was up in the one-sixties when she had her knee done and they just sat her in a quiet room.
[SEG0004] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Mum, stop gripping the arm. Sorry we're late, the car park machine ate my coins and then the school phoned about my youngest.
[SEG0005] person_4 (DOCTOR): Hello Mrs Hale, I'm Dr Okonkwo. Come through and sit yourself down. What's been worrying you most since the operation?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): It's the right hip. Um, six weeks since the replacement and it's still stiff, and I keep thinking I've damaged it.
[SEG0007] person_4 (DOCTOR): Tell me what an ordinary day is like with it.

[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Mornings are the worst, it's stiff till I've walked about a bit. And it aches when I get up from the chair. I'm on the stick the whole time. The wound looks dry to me, I think it's healed.
[SEG0009] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The district nurse last week said the scar was healed. She won't put that stick down, not even indoors.
[SEG0010] person_4 (DOCTOR): And how are you getting on with the pain tablets?

[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): The paracetomol takes the edge off. I take two of the five hundreds, four times a day. Is that too much? I read it wrecks your liver and then I can't switch my brain off.
[SEG0012] person_4 (DOCTOR): Two five-hundred milligram tablets four times a day is the usual full dose, and it won't hurt a healthy liver. You're on the aspirin as well, for the clots?

[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, every morning. They said it stops the clots while I'm not walking far. Do I have to stay on it for the rest of my life, because that's the bit that really scares me?
[SEG0014] person_1 (NURSE): The discharge summary says asprin seventy five milligrams, once a day.
[SEG0015] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No, that's not what we've got at home. The packet in the cupboard is a hundred and fifty, and I've been giving her the hundred and fifty ones.
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh god. Uh, have I been on the wrong dose? Am I going to bleed? Should I stop it tonight?

[SEG0017] person_4 (DOCTOR): Let's not jump ahead. Aspirin makes the platelets less sticky, so a clot is less likely to form in the leg veins while you're pottering with the stick. I can't tell from this chair if you're on seventy five or a hundred and fifty, so keep taking one tablet each morning as you have been, and bring the box in so we can match it to the letter.
[SEG0018] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any swelling in the calf, or one leg bigger than the other?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No, no swelling. I check both legs every night because I'm terrified of a clot. They look the same.
[SEG0020] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any fever, or feeling shivery?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No fever. I haven't felt hot once.
[SEG0022] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any cough, or trouble with your breathing?

[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): The stick catches on the hall rug and I nearly went over yesterday. Should I get one of those trolley frames, or is a stick enough? I don't want to fall and wreck the new hip.
[SEG0024] person_4 (DOCTOR): We'll come to the rug in a minute. On the breathing though, any cough or shortness of breath?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, sorry. No cough. Breathing's been fine.
[SEG0026] person_4 (DOCTOR): And your weight, have you lost any?

[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, I think maybe a little, my rings are looser. But I haven't been on the scales, so I couldn't tell you when that started or how much. Might just be the rings, I don't know.
[SEG0028] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She is eating, Doctor. Porridge in the morning and a proper dinner. I do the cooking.
[SEG0029] person_4 (DOCTOR): Good. May I have a look at the hip and at your calves?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, yes, go on. Will it hurt? I tense up, I can't help it.
[SEG0031] person_4 (DOCTOR): The scar is dry and fully healed, no redness around it. Both calves are soft and the same size, there's no swelling. And you walked in steadily enough on the stick.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): So it's not infected? And it's not a clot? Please say it straight, I need to hear the words.

[SEG0033] person_4 (DOCTOR): I think this is the hip settling after the replacement. The bone and the soft tissues are still knitting onto the new joint, which is why it stays stiff, and I don't see an infection or a clot today.

[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Knitting on, right, so I'm not damaging it? How long does the stiffness last? I live with Claire and she's doing everything, I feel a proper burden. And when am I allowed to drive?
[SEG0035] person_4 (DOCTOR): Err, stiffness at six weeks is very ordinary, and you're not a burden, you're mending. Driving is usually alright once you can manage an emergency stop.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): An emergency stop. I don't think I could, not yet. What if it dislocates in the car? I've read all about dislocation and it keeps me awake.

[SEG0037] person_4 (DOCTOR): Dislocation is uncommon if you don't bend the hip right up or twist on it. So no low soft chairs, and don't cross your legs. If you can't do an emergency stop yet, leave the driving for another fortnight and then see how the leg feels.
[SEG0038] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll shift the hall rug tonight. And she's been sleeping in the dining room, because of the stairs. Is that alright to carry on?
[SEG0039] person_4 (DOCTOR): Downstairs is sensible while you're on the stick. Yes, get that rug up. I'll see you back here in six weeks, and bring the aspirin box with you.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks. What if it gets worse before then? What if the ache turns into proper pain in the night? Do I ring you, or is that A and E?

[SEG0041] person_4 (DOCTOR): If the pain suddenly ramps up, or the wound starts to weep, or a calf swells, ring the surgery the same day, and go to A and E if you can't get through. Otherwise I'll see you here in six weeks.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. Same day, I will. I still feel a bit wobbly about the whole thing, but thank you.
[SEG0043] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll put the box in my handbag now so we don't forget it. Come on then, Mum.

spec.situation: Older patient six weeks after a hip replacement with a daughter; wound healed; walks with a stick; takes aspirin for clots and painkiller; swelling of the calf asked about and denied.

traps.happens: The doctor asks only two to four review-of-systems questions (for example fever, weight, cough). Several other body systems are never asked about. One of the asked questions gets a vague or mixed answer.
traps.label_rule: negative_findings / review_of_systems ONLY for items the doctor actually asked AND the patient answered, evidence = that question and answer. Never add review-of-systems entries for systems nobody asked about, and never cite an unrelated turn (for example a turn about tiredness) for a system review.

traps.happens: The doctor (or nurse) explains a mechanism or a diagnosis in the patient's body ('the voice box is irritated by reflux', 'diabetes dulls the nerves in the feet', 'the swelling is your body fighting infection'). A nurse or caregiver also mentions a fact about THEIR OWN life (their sister, their child, their own illness).
traps.label_rule: Explanations by the doctor are NEVER symptoms, history or social history of the patient; they may only appear as clinical_assessment or counselling if the doctor stated them as such. A nurse's or caregiver's own life facts are not recorded as the patient's. Each symptom's reported_by is the person who really described it.

features: disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.
patient_answers_other_question: the patient answers a different question than the one asked, and the doctor repeats or lets it go.
